title: Direct laser-written optomechanical double membranes in an optical microcavity
authors: Lukas Tenbrake, Daniel Stachanow, Florian Giefer, Jana Blechmann, Wolfgang Alt, Sebastian Hofferberth, Hannes Pfeifer
abstract: Optomechanical membrane-in-the-middle systems that comprise several coupled compliant membranes offer enhanced optomechanical coupling and collective dynamics. Recent realizations were fundamentally restricted to two membranes and to limited structural optimization of the involved membranes due to their intricate fabrication and experimental integration. Here, we present a fiber-based Fabry-Perot microcavity incorporating monolithically integrated double-membrane resonators fabricated by 3D direct laser writing. We realize controllable mechanical mode hybridization of membranes with coupling rates of up to $J_{\mathrm{mech}}/2π= 0.16$ MHz, exceeding the mechanical linewidths. We demonstrate enhanced collective optomechanical coupling of the membrane stack's breathing mode, reaching collective coupling strengths of up to $g_{\mathrm{col}}^{(-)}/2π\approx 0.1$ MHz. Our transfer-matrix calculations predict further substantial enhancements with realistic reductions of membrane thickness and spacing, and a larger number of membranes. Our results establish direct laser-written membrane arrays as a scalable platform for multimode cavity optomechanics, combining tunable mechanical interactions, enhanced collective optomechanical coupling, and scalability towards larger mechanically coupled resonator systems.
summary: This paper reports on the creation of double-membrane resonators within an optical microcavity using 3D direct laser writing. By engineering mechanical mode hybridization, the researchers achieved enhanced collective optomechanical coupling, establishing a scalable platform for studying multimode cavity optomechanics. The combination of advanced nanofabrication and rigorous theoretical modeling makes this system highly relevant for quantum sensing and quantum light-matter interaction studies.
main_problem: The research aims to overcome the limitation of optomechanical systems being restricted to only two coupled membranes by establishing a scalable platform for multimode cavity optomechanics.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated double-membrane resonators in a fiber-based microcavity using 3D direct laser writing, achieving enhanced collective optomechanical coupling strengths up to $g_{col}/2\pi \approx 0.1$ MHz.
method: The study combines experimental fabrication using 3D direct laser writing with theoretical modeling using finite-element methods (FEM) and transfer-matrix calculations to predict and analyze coupling strengths.
model_or_system: The system is a fiber-based Fabry-Perot microcavity containing monolithically integrated double-membrane resonators. The physics involves mechanical mode hybridization induced by physical coupling legs, leading to distinct center-of-mass and breathing normal modes.
key_observables: Collective optomechanical coupling strengths ($g_{col}$), mechanical mode splitting ($J_{mech}$), and cavity finesse ($F$).
important_parameters: Membrane thickness ($t_{mem}$), membrane-to-membrane spacing ($s_{mem}$), and the angle of the connecting support legs ($	heta_{leg}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the transfer-matrix formalism treating the system as a 1D multilayer cavity, and mechanical simulations required correcting the dynamic modulus by a scaling factor (0.88).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system schematic, SEM images of the fabricated structure, mode diagrams showing hybridized modes, and cross-sectional cuts mapping the wavelength dependence of collective coupling strengths and cavity finesse.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from demonstrating the fabrication of double-membrane resonators via DLW, to modeling the mechanical mode hybridization using FEM, and finally characterizing the enhanced collective optomechanical coupling and its wavelength dependence using transfer-matrix calculations.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly tunable, scalable platform for cavity optomechanics by engineering mechanical coupling, which is crucial for studying collective dynamics and realizing complex quantum light-matter interactions beyond simple two-mode systems.
